abstract: The NIH BRAIN Initiative Cell Atlas Network (BICAN) is developing a standardized, integrated reference framework for classifying and studying brain cell types across human, macaque, marmoset, and mouse. We present a cross-species, multimodal atlas of the basal ganglia, a group of subcortical nuclei central to motor control, adaptive behavior, and neurological disease. Built from large-scale single-cell transcriptomic classification and integrated with epigenomic, spatial genomic, multiomic, and developmental datasets, the atlas provides a curated, data-driven taxonomy with standardized nomenclature, extensive phenotypic characterization, and community-informed annotation. Cell types are mapped into species-specific anatomical reference frameworks and linked across species through structural ontologies. Realizing this resource required coordinated standards for tissue acquisition and processing, harmonized donor metadata, anatomical registration, sequencing pipelines, data infrastructure, visualization, mapping tools, and interoperable metadata. The BICAN basal ganglia atlas demonstrates how pipelines and standards can be implemented, validated, and scaled toward a whole-brain human and mammalian cell-type reference.
title: Toward an integrated framework for a human and mammalian brain cell atlas

abstract: Juvenile social play is critical for neurodevelopment, yet the neural mechanisms organizing moment-to-moment interactions remain elusive. Using social behavior sequencing (Social-seq)-an occlusion-robust 3D pose estimation and unsupervised clustering pipeline-we found that nucleus accumbens (NAc) dopamine was tightly coupled to sub-second social syllables during naturalistic interactions. In wild-type juveniles, males exhibited a sharper dopaminergic contrast between proactive play and forced submission than females did, consistent with sex-divergent play strategies. In Shank3-deficient autism models, this process was fundamentally corrupted: proactive play-evoked dopamine responses were abolished in males and significantly sign-inverted in females, with male-specific enhancements during non-social behaviors, driving social play deficits. A multi-agent reinforcement learning model parameterized by disrupted, play-related dopaminergic reinforcement values recapitulated mutant phenotypes. Closed-loop optogenetic stimulation of ventral tegmental area (VTA)-NAc dopamine projections, time-locked to proactive play, restored reciprocal play in Shank3-deficient rats. Sub-second dopaminergic reinforcement thus orchestrates naturalistic social behavior, providing a behaviorally contingent interventional framework for neurodevelopmental disorders.
title: Sub-second dopamine reinforcement shapes juvenile social play

abstract: Chronic kidney disease (CKD) represents a major medical burden. Diabetic kidney disease (DKD) is a leading cause of CKD, but intracellular pathways that can be pharmacologically targeted are poorly defined. Using transcriptome screening of DKD model mice we found that a carbohydrate-responsive element–binding protein (ChREBP)-dependent transcriptional cascade is markedly up-regulated in diabetic kidneys. Genetic ablation of ChREBP in diabetic mice ameliorated DKD, establishing ChREBP as a potential causal driver. A chemical screen based on ChREBP transcriptional activity identified D-532 as a small-molecule inhibitor that is effective in human and rodent cells. Oral administration of D-532 protected multiple diabetic mouse models from DKD progression and suppressed ChREBP and its downstream targets, including genes associated with excessive reactive oxygen species production. These findings position ChREBP as a pharmacologically targetable transcriptional driver of DKD and provide proof of concept that ChREBP inhibition can confer renal protection.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: ChREBP drives diabetic kidney disease, and its inhibition confers renal protection

abstract: Temporal control of neuronal differentiation is essential for establishing stable neuronal identities, yet the transcriptional and epigenetic mechanisms underlying this process remain poorly understood. Using auditory neurons as an in vivo model, we investigate the role of the proneural factor NEUROD1 in regulating neuronal differentiation timing and subtype specification. To bypass early neuronal loss in germline Neurod1 deletion mutants, we generated a delayed, self-terminating conditional knockout mouse ( Neurod1ST ) that permits analysis of later differentiation stages. Integration of NEUROD1 chromatin binding and histone profiling at embryonic day (E) 11.5 with transcriptomic analyses across E11.5, E14.5, and E18.5 reveals a two-phase regulatory program during auditory neuron development that parallels dynamic Neurod1 expression. In the first phase, coinciding with Neurod1 upregulation during early neuronal differentiation, NEUROD1 preferentially binds putative enhancers of neuronal differentiation genes and promotes their transition to active chromatin states, consistent with pioneer factor activity. Loss of Neurod1 disrupts these epigenomic transitions, resulting in persistence of progenitor-like states with premature activation of differentiation and axonogenesis programs. This dysregulation is accompanied by activation of alternative regulatory networks, leading to defective neuronal migration and innervation, progressive identity instability, and apoptosis. In the second phase, marked by reexpression of Neurod1 in developing Type Ib/Ic precursors, Neurod1 deletion selectively impairs Type Ic specification while promoting a Type Ib-like identity. These findings identify NEUROD1 as a temporal regulator that coordinates developmental progression and stabilizes auditory neuron identity through phased regulatory activity, providing a mechanistic framework for how pioneer transcription factors couple chromatin remodeling to developmental timing.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Two-phase NEUROD1 pioneer activity synchronizes sensory neuronal differentiation and subtype specification

abstract: In this study, we reveal long-tail dynamics spontaneously arising from a magnetic system. Specifically, we consider a classical spin system and demonstrate the emergence of a spin-ice physics when drive-induced heating is well suppressed. We show that at high driving frequencies, magnetic monopole excitations exhibit nonergodic stochastic dynamics characterized by power-law-distributed trapping times with long tails—a behavior that persists even in the absence of driving. At intermediate driving frequencies, the system eventually heats up to an infinite-temperature state. However, contrary to conventional wisdom of Floquet heating, the heating time in our model is extremely sensitive to different initial-state realizations and also follows a long-tailed power-law distribution, which arise specifically due to periodic driving. We show that an effective short-range attractive interaction between monopoles is responsible for the long-tailed distributions observed in both monopole and heating dynamics.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Emergent long-tailed dynamics in spin ice

abstract: Whether and how people approach social interactions hinges on how they expect others to respond. Extensive social psychology research suggests that people are inaccurate interpersonal perceivers, overestimating negative responses (e.g., discomfort) and underestimating positive responses (e.g., appreciation) across a variety of social situations. However, this conclusion is based almost exclusively on mean-level bias analyses that obscure the dyadic nature of interpersonal judgment and rely on a narrow conceptualization of interpersonal accuracy. Leveraging research on favor-asking and anticipated compliance as an exemplar, we demonstrate that interpersonal accuracy takes multiple theoretically distinct forms, and that the prevailing conclusion that people misunderstand their influence over others—because they tend to underestimate compliance—is likely overgeneralized. Across four studies (13,196 directed dyadic ratings), we show that people accurately differentiate between who will comply with their favor requests (dyadic meta-accuracy) despite the average tendency to underestimate compliance (mean-level bias). This pattern emerged for specific and general favor requests, among well- and newly-acquainted individuals, and beyond what could be expected due to self-projection. Through this dyadic lens, people are highly adept judges of their influence over others, as they are able to target their requests toward individuals who are uniquely likely to acquiesce to them—and can avoid wasting time on those who are not. Thus, our research refines existing implications for how people approach asking for favors. More broadly, by aligning theory, measurement, and level of analysis, our studies elucidate the need for greater theoretical precision and empirical breadth in interpersonal accuracy research.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: People know who to ask for favors despite underestimating compliance

abstract: Continuum elastic shells with residual stresses can exhibit complex motions that require vanishing elastic energy to excite, also called geometric zero modes, enabling them to be driven by weak and generic energy inputs. Despite recent interest in these modes, we understand very little about their dynamical properties. Plates with a curved, rather than flat, in-plane geometry, also called non-Euclidean plates, are one example in which residual stresses and geometry combine to produce a continuum of ground states. The plate can explore these states through a geometric zero mode when it has the shape of a minimal surface—a surface with zero mean curvature. We demonstrate that a non-Euclidean plate with the shape of a saddle minimal surface exhibits the predicted continuous stability, but this degeneracy is ultimately lifted by aging. Despite developing a preferred configuration, the zero mode remains the softest mode. Using a combination of analytical theory and experiments, we show that the elastodynamics of this soft mode is captured by the dynamics of a damped pendulum. A periodic driving uncovers resonance phenomena in this pendulum mode, such as small oscillations and steady rotations, but mixes with an additional flapping mode at high frequencies.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Dynamical geometric modes in non-Euclidean plates

abstract: Both p300 acetyltransferase inhibitors and bromodomain inhibitors show therapeutic promise in cancer, but they mostly exhibit limited efficacy and may elicit severe adverse effects due to their lack of targeting selectivity. Thus, selectively disrupting p300 interactions with specific pro-oncogenic targets that are specifically expressed in neoplastic cells could serve as a safe and effective strategy for cancer treatment. Here, we demonstrate that p300 interacts with the pro-oncogenic transcription factor, ZEB1, and catalyzes its acetylation at an evolutionarily conserved K80 residue, stabilizing its expression in aggressive cancer cells. Ectopic expression of wild-type ZEB1 (mostly in acetylated status) but not the acetylation-deficient ZEB1 mutant modulates cytokinome of cancer cells, creating an immune-suppressive tumor microenvironment to support cancer progression. Underlining the importance of ZEB1 posttranslational processing, the K80-acetylated transcription factor is highly expressed in human cancers where its high-level expression is associated with poor prognosis. Importantly, we identify a small molecule compound, WY6, that undergoes high-affinity binding to p300 TAZ2 domain (a domain critical for ZEB1 binding) and consequently disrupts ZEB1 binding to p300, thereby suppressing K80 acetylation. WY6 treatment of tumor cells effectively represses p300-mediated ZEB1 acetylation, promoting its ubiquitination and subsequent degradation. Moreover, in vivo, WY6 potently suppresses orthotopic tumor growth without eliciting obvious toxic side effects and exhibits a synergetic effect when combined with PD-1/PD-L1 blockade immunotherapy. Collectively, our data demonstrate that selective disrupting of p300 and ZEB1 interaction effectively prevents tumor progression and may offer a promising therapeutic strategy for p300–ZEB1 axis-driven malignancies.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Selectively disrupting lysine acetyltransferase p300 and ZEB1 interaction prevents tumor progression while enhancing antitumor immunity

abstract: Cells mechanically interact through the deformations they generate in their surrounding extracellular matrix. We present an analytical theory of the elastic interactions between cells that actively adapt their forces in response to local deformations of their environment. Cells are represented as localized contractile force generators, modeled as polarizable point force dipoles, whose adaptive forces are determined self-consistently with those of surrounding cells. Analysis of the associated elastic interaction energy identifies a generic short-ranged interaction arising from the mutual adaptation of cellular forces. This induced-dipole interaction is analogous to the van der Waals interaction between molecules and likewise is shown to be generally attractive for cells that enhance contractility in response to stretch. Furthermore, unlike the long-ranged elastic interaction between nonpolarizable force-dipoles, that peaks at intermediate matrix stiffness and then weakens as the matrix softens, the induced-dipole interaction strengthens monotonically as the matrix softens and can reverse the interaction from being repulsive at long cell distances to being attractive at short separations. Analytical calculations are presented to illustrate the mutual polarization of forces in pairs of interacting cells on a substrate. The identification of a generic, short-range cohesive elastic interaction between cells is important for understanding cell behavior at short separations and provides a physical mechanism driving cell accumulation on soft substrates.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Elastic interactions of mechanically polarizable cells

abstract: Public health recommendations often advise people to isolate when infected with influenza-like illness (ILI) with the goal of promoting physical distancing and limiting face-to-face interactions when risk of transmission is highest. Because isolation may have negative consequences, it is important to carefully assess whether encouragement to physically distance actually prevents cases of ILI. College campuses can be especially vulnerable to outbreaks of ILI and are ideal environments for assessing the impact of encouragement-to-physically-distance interventions. The eX-FLU cluster-randomized trial followed 579 students on a college campus over a ten-week period during flu season to evaluate such an intervention. Students in the trial were randomized to receive the intervention—encouragement to isolate in their dorm room when symptomatic for ILI—or control. Evaluating the effect of this intervention is challenging because of dependence between students in the trial and an anticipated spillover effect of the intervention. Moreover, while the intervention was designed to affect both face-to-face interactions and ILI infections, the effect on ILI infections is of primary public health interest. In this paper, a randomization-based testing procedure is proposed to assess the intervention effect specifically on ILI infections in the presence of dependent data and spillover effects. The testing procedure is shown theoretically and empirically to control the type I error rate and have good statistical power to detect an intervention effect in trials similar to eX-FLU. When applied to the eX-FLU data, this testing procedure gives moderate evidence that the intervention reduced ILI infections.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Physical distancing to prevent influenza-like illness on a college campus: The eX-FLU trial

abstract: We investigate the spin-interaction energy spectrum of spin turbulence in a driven spinor Bose-Einstein condensate. Continuous spin driving of a spin-1 condensate produces a nonequilibrium steady state with spatially fluctuating magnetization. We observe a power-law scaling consistent with the $-7/3$ exponent predicted for spin-wave turbulence, which persists across our full range of drive strengths despite substantial changes in the spectral anisotropy. After switching off the drive, we track the free-decay evolution and find evidence consistent with a direct cascade of spin-interaction energy toward higher wavenumbers. These results establish an energy-spectral hallmark of spin turbulence and enable quantitative studies of cascade dynamics in spinor superfluids.
title: Energy spectra and cascade in the spin turbulence of a driven spinor Bose-Einstein condensate

abstract: The performance of solid-state $^{229}\text{Th}$ nuclear clocks depends sensitively on the microscopic environment of the thorium nucleus in the host crystal. Here we reassess the dominant quadrupole-split thorium site in $^{229}\text{Th:CaF}_2$, which has been assigned to a thorium dimer in recent spectroscopic work. Thermodynamic estimates, density functional theory calculations, and electric-field-gradient comparisons instead favor an isolated $\text{Th}^{4+}$ substitution on a $\text{Ca}^{2+}$ site charge-compensated by two nearby fluorine interstitials in a relaxed $90^\circ$ motif. The same calculation identifies a higher-energy mixed-shell interstitial motif as a plausible minor site. The clock-active quadrupole-split site is therefore controlled by local fluoride compensation rather than unavoidable thorium aggregation. This defect assignment also has implications for achievable linewidths and provides a microscopic basis for reducing broadening in solid-state nuclear clocks.
title: Defect assignment of the clock site in 229 Th:CaF 2

abstract: Precision measurements of time-reversal (T) symmetry violating moments probe physics beyond the Standard Model. We show that precision spectroscopy of paramagnetic lanthanide and actinide ions doped into noncentrosymmetric crystals offers a promising platform for extending the sensitivity of searches for T-violation in nuclear physics. The unpaired valence electron in these ions allows the engineering of highly-coherent hyperfine transitions that are insensitive to magnetic fields, yet highly sensitive to new physics. These systems also provide other advantages for new physics searches, including large numbers of ions that can be measured in doped crystals, strong electric polarization of the ions by the crystal fields, enhancement of T-violating nuclear moments in nonspherical nuclei, and accurate comagnetometers generated by crystal symmetry. We estimate the new physics sensitivity of these proposed systems to be two orders of magnitude better than existing constraints.
title: Sensing T -violating nuclear moments of paramagnetic ions in crystals

abstract: We propose Higgsino dark matter as a potential interpretation of the $248~\mathrm{keV}$ nuclear-recoil event of interest reported by the LUX-ZEPLIN (LZ) experiment. LZ studied several rare background processes and detector effects in detail, but did not identify any as a likely explanation of the event. A nearly pure Higgsino naturally realizes inelastic dark matter through the off-diagonal $Z$ coupling of two nearly degenerate neutral Majorana states separated by a mass splitting $δ$. The same electroweak interaction fixes the inelastic Higgsino-nucleon scattering cross section, rather than leaving it as a free parameter. We show that the predicted Higgsino inelastic scattering cross section approaches the published LZ two-sided 90% confidence interval for a Higgsino mass $m_{\widetilde H}\sim1~\mathrm{TeV}$ and a mass splitting $δ\sim350~\mathrm{keV}$.
title: Higgsino dark matter interpretation of the LUX-ZEPLIN 248 keV nuclear-recoil event

abstract: Programmable photonic quantum processors face a critical challenge: despite significant advances in quantum state preparation and manipulation, measurements remain limited to projective techniques. Here, we demonstrate a programmable measurement processor that overcomes this limitation by enabling arbitrary quantum measurements within a scalable circuit framework. Our large-scale integrated photonic architecture achieves precise coherent control of ancillary quantum systems, realizing a universal four-dimensional quantum measurement device. We benchmark the processor by performing measurement tomography on 100 randomly selected measurements, achieving an average fidelity of 97.7%. The processor's performance exceeds the theoretical limits of projective measurements in three key quantum information tasks: state discrimination (with 23 times lower error), state estimation (with 10.6% higher fidelity), and randomness generation (with 37% more randomness yield), demonstrating its high operational quality. This work establishes a fully programmable quantum measurement processor, advancing the development of universal quantum operations for photonic quantum information processing by providing the key missing component.
title: Single programmable photonic circuit for universal quantum measurements

abstract: It has been shown that static black hole event horizons cannot exist in time-dependent backgrounds without becoming naked singularities. In light of this, we are left with the question ``how does a black hole horizon evolve in an expanding universe?'' Here we offer a solution to this puzzle by showing in full generality that regular black hole apparent horizons tend to become comoving, thus confirming the necessity of a cosmological coupling and raising intriguing possibilities for the early growth of black holes.
title: Black hole apparent horizons become comoving with the universe

abstract: Stroboscopic measurements of a time-dependent projector generate a quantum Zeno dynamics whose effective Hamiltonian is the Kato-Avron Hamiltonian for parallel transport, which reduces to counterdiabatic driving in the case of a nonselective measurement of the instantaneous eigenprojectors of the system. The same generator arises under continuous monitoring of a time-dependent observable and under a time-varying complex absorbing potential. Departures from the ideal Zeno limit are governed, in all three settings, by a single positive leakage operator with a dynamical and a purely geometric contribution. Matching the corresponding generators yields a model-independent generalized Schulman relation for the quantum Zeno dynamics in the three scenarios, and a purely geometric bound on the measurement resources needed to steer a subspace along a prescribed path.
title: Shortcuts to adiabaticity via adaptive quantum Zeno measurements

abstract: We prove a singularity theorem in semiclassical gravity without assuming global hyperbolicity or the null energy/curvature condition; the former is replaced by the weaker causality conditions of stable causality and past reflectivity, and the latter is replaced as is standard by the Generalized Second Law. This establishes in particular that the standard models of evaporating black holes are singular - i.e. they are null geodesically incomplete.
title: Quantum singularity theorem for the evaporating black hole

abstract: Precise measurements of the metastable helium (1s)(2s)$\,^3S_1$ ionization energy have revealed a 9$σ$ discrepancy with QED theory that persists in isotopic measurements, suggesting a leptophilic bosonic interaction as a possible explanation. A subsequent investigation of such interactions has concluded that only a scalar boson interaction is consistent with the He observations. Taking this as a starting point, we derive the response of positronium energy levels to the corresponding finite-range Yukawa potential, using exact hydrogenic matrix elements and a numerical helium calculation. Across the viable mediator-mass range of 0-800 eV, the He anomaly interpreted in this way implies a positronium 1$^3$S$_1 \rightarrow 2^3$S$_1$ shift ranging from 0.250-0.850 MHz, and a 2S-ionization shift of 0.14-0.21 MHz. We discuss the feasibility of observing these shifts experimentally.
title: Precision positronium spectroscopy as a test of the helium ionization energy anomaly

abstract: We show analytically that the convergence of the QNM expansion of the retarded Green's function of the Schwarzschild spacetime is set by a singularity in the complex time plane. The singularity has a simple geometric origin: it is an example of a `bouncing singularity' in the language of AdS/CFT literature, caused by a null geodesic which bounces from the black hole singularity. Our work explains why the QNM convergence region at real times is bounded by null ray which scatters from the gravitational potential at a seemingly unremarkable point ($r_* = 0$ in the conventions of previous work) -- this ray is the same distance from the origin as the bouncing singularity in the relevant complex plane. The same set of singularities are responsible for an annular region of convergence for the Matsubara mode sum which describes the early time behaviour of the Schwarzschild Green's function for perturbations close to the horizon.
title: Bouncing singularities in Schwarzschild geometry: A geometric origin of the quasinormal mode convergence region

abstract: Ultracold Bose gases in one-dimensional optical lattices constitute an important benchmark problem in the study of strongly interacting many-body quantum phases. Here we present a combined experimental and theoretical study of their phase-coherence properties over a wide range of lattice depths. Experimentally, we extract the single-particle correlation function directly from the measured momentum distribution. Theoretically, we perform tensor-network simulations of the Bose-Hubbard model that incorporate all relevant experimental parameters. For deep lattices well within the Mott insulator regime, the experimental results are in good agreement with the expected zero-temperature behavior, with only small temperature-dependent corrections. As the lattice depth is reduced, finite-temperature effects become increasingly important. We find that the experimental data are quantitatively described by an effective temperature extracted from the tensor-network simulations, and that this effective temperature decreases markedly with increasing lattice depth. Rather than indicating actual cooling, we interpret this behavior as evidence of inhibition of thermalization caused by the formation of Mott domains that suppress heat transport. Counterintuitively, the inhibition of thermalization favors the preparation of an effectively low-entropy quantum gas in the trap center for large lattice depths.
title: Phase coherence of strongly interacting bosons in one-dimensional optical lattices

abstract: A locking between propagation direction $\hat{\bf q}$, spin $\hat{\bf S}$, and surface or interface normal $\hat{\bf n}$ -- a phenomenon broadly termed \textit{chirality} -- pervades evanescent or surface waves in optics, magnetism, plasmonics, and acoustics. Yet, it is not known whether the phenomenon is universal or bound to conditions. Here, we unveil that any \textit{source-free} vector field that propagates along $\hat{\bf q}$ and is evanescent along $\hat{\bf n}$, the existence of a spin automatically enforces a rigid, right-handed locking among $\hat{\bf q}$, $\hat{\bf S}$, and $\hat{\bf n}$, that is characterized by a chirality index $C_{\bf q}\equiv \hat{\bf n}\cdot(\hat{\bf S}\times \hat{\bf q})>0$. For an arbitrary propagation direction defined by $\hat{\bf q}\cdot \hat{\bf S}\equiv η\in [-1,1]$, i.e., not necessarily transverse spin, we derive a fundamental upper bound $C_{\bf q}\le \sqrt{1-η^2}$. The universal absence of left-handed evanescent (source-less) vector fields underscores the fundamental physical non-equivalence of mirror-image configurations -- a principle echoed by parity violation, the natural excess of enantiomers in chiral molecules, and the fixed chirality of DNA.
title: Universal right-hand chirality of evanescent vector fields

abstract: The collisional properties of lanthanides exhibit remarkable complexity due to their many valence electrons, leading to an extraordinarily dense Feshbach spectrum showing signs of quantum chaos. Here we explore the situation of bosonic spin mixtures of erbium, adding the additional spin degree of freedom to the problem. We detect several inter- and intra-spin scattering resonances, exhibiting a peculiar asymmetric shape with a pronounced loss minimum. By developing a simplified multi-channel model we are able to recreate this characteristic behavior and to trace its origin to destructive interference between multiple pathways as predicted by Fano. We additionally observe a series of Fano-Feshbach resonances across multiple spin channels connected to the same molecular state, again confirmed by our theory. Our work opens the door for a detailed investigation to study multi-spin strongly-coupled scattering phenomena.
title: Observation of Fano-suppression in scattering resonances of bosonic erbium atoms
